one_liner: Binary serializer for plain Nim types; ~38x faster serialize, ~36x faster deserialize than JSON-based std/marshal.
what_it_does: flatty turns Nim values (numbers, strings, seqs, arrays, tuples, objects including private fields and object variants, refs, Table/OrderedTable/CountTable, HashSet, Option, distinct and range types) into a compact binary string and back. The API is two calls: `x.toFlatty()` returns a string and `s.fromFlatty(T)` rebuilds a `T`; there is no schema or IDL, because the Nim type is the schema. The package also ships binny (a side-effect-free StringStream replacement over a string), hashy (hash any object through its flatty bytes), hexprint and a UTF-16/UTF-32 encode module.
how_it_is_fast: Encoding and decoding are generic overloads resolved at compile time per type, while std/marshal walks runtime type info (`typeinfo.Any`), writes JSON text and records every ref address in an IntSet. For seqs and arrays whose element type is 'flat' (supportsCopyMem, no pointers, variants, ranges or int-width mismatch), flatty writes a length prefix and moves the whole block with one copyMem; strings are also one copyMem, and decode allocates with newStringUninit/setLenUninit to skip zero-fill. Output is appended to a plain string with setLen plus copyMem instead of StringStream, values keep native little-endian layout with no byte swapping, and hot procs are `{.inline.}`.
when_to_use: Nim-to-Nim messages or save files where both ends are built from the same type definitions, e.g. game state over UDP with netty plus supersnappy compression (the stack the README describes).
Payloads dominated by seqs/arrays of numbers or flat objects, which encode and decode as a single memcpy per container.
Snapshotting acyclic ref-object trees: about 2.3 ms to serialize an 11,125-node tree in the README benchmark.
Decoding untrusted network blobs: since the July 2026 hardening, every read is bounds-checked (also under -d:danger), length prefixes are validated before allocation, and a fuzzer runs in tests.
Hashing arbitrary nested Nim objects by content with the bundled hashy module.
when_not_to_use: Data read by non-Nim programs: the format is defined only by Nim types, with no IDL and no other-language implementation (the JS target is Nim-compiled JS only).
Long-lived storage while types evolve: the README says there is no versioning, so any change to a type breaks reading old blobs.

Graphs with shared or cyclic refs: `toFlatty` on a ref writes a nil flag plus the value with no identity tracking, so shared refs come back as copies and cycles recurse until the stack overflows. std/marshal tracks ref addresses and keeps both.
Big-endian targets (compile-time error) or JS builds with int64/uint64 fields, which the README says are supported badly.

Polymorphic ref hierarchies or variants with more than one `case` discriminator: encoding follows the static type, and objvar.nim reads only the first discriminator (PR #36 for multiple/nested discriminators was closed unmerged).

integration.min_toolchain: Nim >= 2.0.0 (flatty.nimble); install with nimble or atlas
integration.platforms: Little-endian native targets only (compile error on big-endian); CI on Linux, macOS and Windows plus the Nim JS backend under Node; the decode stack guard is off on emscripten and unrecognized platforms
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Procs work on caller-owned strings, and the only global state is a `{.threadvar.}` stack limit, so separate buffers on separate threads look safe by inspection.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the call swap is one line (`$$x` to `x.toFlatty`, `to[T](s)` to `s.fromFlatty(T)`), but the binary format cannot read existing std/marshal JSON and does not preserve shared or cyclic refs

gotchas: Blobs are build-dependent: `int`/`uint` and lengths use the target's native width unless both sides compile with the same -d:flatty32 or -d:flatty64, copyable seq/array elements are raw memory images (sizeof(T) each, padding included), and every enum is written as 8 bytes.
Malformed input raises FlattyError (bad length, count or enum), IndexDefect (truncation) or RangeDefect (range type out of bounds); the README tells you to catch both CatchableError and Defect.
The README benchmark predates the July 2026 hardening (PR #55), which itself reports ref-tree deserialize ~1.4-1.5x slower afterwards; serialize is unchanged.

Much of the gap to std/marshal is marshal's reflection, not binary vs text: in the same table jsony (JSON) serializes in 9.618 ms, ~8.9x faster than marshal, while the binary peer bingo is only ~16% slower than flatty on serialize (min).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Every catalogued sibling targets another language (Rust, Go, C#, C++, Zig); none is a Nim library, so pick flatty inside a Nim-only system. Pick a cross-language schema format such as Bebop or SBE instead when non-Nim peers must read the data or the schema must evolve, since flatty has no IDL and no versioning.
verified_claims_summary: The README's benchy table (100 runs each) for an 11,125-node ref-object tree shows serialize 2.265 ms vs 85.178 ms for std/marshal's JSON `$$` (~37.6x on min, ~38.6x on average) and deserialize 2.643 ms vs 148.723 ms (~56x on min, ~36x on average). Nim version, compiler flags and hardware are not stated (tests/config.nims only sets --path), and the numbers were recorded before the PR #55 hardening, so current deserialize is likely nearer 24-40x (derived from PR #55's 1.4-1.5x slowdown).
status_note: Active: nimble version 0.4.0, last commit 2026-08-13, decode path fuzzed and hardened in July 2026; MIT, pure Nim with no dependencies, small enough to vendor.
